rv.q: Written by Colman Domingo and Patricia McGregor, the formally ambitious, if muddled, “Lights Out: Nat ‘King’ Cole” takes place on that fateful Dec. 17, 1957, when the pianist and singer said goodbye to his audience.
And while not technically a musical, it offers some of the most delightful music, and singing, available on New York’s stages at the moment.
Commercial breaks, projected on a screen and performed onstage are both delightfully amusing to watch and a penetrating commentary on life in America at that time.
There’s more than a glimmer of a great show in Lights Out: Nat “King” Cole, anchored by an excellent Dulé Hill and a showstopping Daniel J. Watts.
Lights Out is admirable for trying to take the biomusical in a new direction rather than hoofing down a familiar path, but in the end, it leaves us in the dark.
But the overall production is so disjointed and preachy that it winds up diminishing the figure at its center.
Colman Domingo and Patricia McGregor have written a deliciously dark masterpiece in this unforgettable production...
It’s worth a trip to the East Village.

“Lights Out: Nat King Cole” attempts to be a different kind of jukebox bio-musical. More than a series of wonderful songs, sung by fine performers, it seeks to deliver some important messages: unfortunately they got a bit muddled along the way.
Lights Out is a showcase for some wonderful song and dance, but the luster dims whenever the band stops playing.

cn.t: Hill and Watts deliver strong performances in this formally ambitious but muddled biomusical about Nat King Cole's groundbreaking TV show. Critics praise its dark exploration of racism but find the "fever dream" structure disjointed and befuddling.

vr.q: Although I can't quite put my finger on it, I really enjoyed it and I would recommend going in with the intention to just experience it in the moment
I really dug what they were doing here
